slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open by naming the central question: can the players move in either order and still get the same value? The class should distinguish the automatic weak inequality from the much stronger equality. The saddle point is the certificate that both orders have met at one value.

slides.title: Two Orders
slides.notes: Spend time on the order of quantifiers. Minimax and maximin are not two spellings of the same expression. One lets the maximizing variable respond after x, the other lets the minimizing variable respond after y. Equality requires geometric structure or a saddle certificate.

slides.title: Weak Inequality
slides.notes: This slide is the baseline. The lower value can never exceed the upper value, regardless of convexity. The interesting minimax theorem begins when the gap is zero and the two orders agree. That is the analog of strong duality in this saddle-function language.

slides.title: Saddle Certificate
slides.notes: Give students the exact certificate they should try to verify. A saddle point satisfies two one-sided optimality statements. It is a maximum in y along one slice and a minimum in x along the other. Those two inequalities squeeze the lower and upper values together.

slides.title: Convex Concave Hypotheses
slides.notes: Separate shape from attainment. Convexity in the minimizing variable and concavity in the maximizing variable are what make the saddle geometry plausible. Compactness, closedness, or level-set control are different assumptions: they keep the relevant extrema from escaping.

slides.title: Box Example
slides.notes: Use the example as a laboratory rather than a theorem substitute. The payoff is convex in x and concave in y, and the stationary equations meet at the center of the box. The slice shapes make it plausible that the two orders agree, while the numerical check can confirm the common value.

slides.title: Failure Modes
slides.notes: Use this slide to avoid turning minimax equality into a wish. Equality can fail because extrema escape, because the payoff lacks the right convex-concave shape, or because boundary restrictions produce a genuine gap. Each failure corresponds to a different theorem hypothesis.

slides.title: Numerical Checker
slides.notes: Tie the slide directly to the notebook check. The computation should not merely find a plausible saddle point; it should compare both optimization orders. A small residual supports the equality claim, while a positive residual means the sequential games have different values.

slides.title: Learner Lab
slides.notes: Frame the lab as an order-of-optimization experiment. Students should perturb one ingredient, compute the two sequential values, and only then decide whether a saddle interpretation remains valid. The explanation should identify whether equality survived, moved to the boundary, or failed because a hypothesis broke.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: Close with the checklist students should reuse. First compare the upper and lower values. Then look for a saddle point that certifies both inequalities. Finally check the shape and attainment hypotheses, because those are the assumptions that turn the weak inequality into equality.
